newsitem.title: UK: UK shares outlook - FTSE 100 set for new peaks.
newsitem.headline: UK shares outlook - FTSE 100 set for new peaks.

text.p: Leading British stocks look set to continue their post-election euphoria next week, underpinned by soaring financial shares and the new Labour government's radical move to give the Bank of England greater independence.
Nick Glydon, a chart analyst at Robert Fleming Securities, said there was no reason why the financials shouldn't continue to support the broader market for the near future.
Glydon said the 4,800 level looked like a reachable target for the UK's benchmark FTSE 100 index, which on Friday surged to the latest of a series of record highs.
"The market is looking overbought and the breadth is bad, but the fact that it has continued rising means we're not unduly worried," Glydon said.
The FTSE 100 has enjoyed eight straight sessions of gains since Labour's landslide poll victory in the May 1 election, rising some six percent.

An unprecedented shortage of stock in the banking sector has underpinned the broader market as institutions scrambled to increase their sector weightings ahead of the flotation of Britain's biggest building society, the Halifax, in June.
Coupled with bid speculation surrounding newly floated Alliance & Leicester Plc, the financials - which make up 20 percent of total market capitalisation - have been propelled to record highs.

Also likely to carry on underpinning sentiment was the decision this week by the new government to impose an early rise in interest rates, coupled with the surprise announcement that the Bank of England will have more freedom to set monetary policy.
Panmure Gordon was the first major brokerage to publicly raise its year-end FTSE forecast to 5,000 from 4,500, reflecting the market's upbeat response to the monetary reforms.
"Gordon Brown's decision to hand over control of UK monetary policy to the Bank of England is unequivocally good news for UK asset markets," said Panmure Gordon economist Stuart Weatherby.
"The extent of the increase in interest rates required to slow the economy should now be reduced."

Analysts said that even though the Bank may be more inclined to take a pre-emptive monetary stance, there was a growing feeling that fiscal policy will take the bulk of the strain. But the government's plans will remain unknown until a mini-budget in July.
Richard Jeffrey, strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, said that until something happened to change these perceptions, the market was likely to push higher.

"The expectation on the inflation front is that everything will remain calm for the time being," he said. "Politics and the changes in monetary policy have been taken positively and we have very strong institutional cash flow."
Economic data including unemployment and average earnings figures on Wednesday and retail prices on Thursday could help provide further clues on the state of the British economy, Jeffrey said.
"We are seeing quite a severe tightening in the labour market which is beginning to put upwards pressure on average earnings, and this is particularly true of the service sector."
But the market will perhaps be more sensitive to events in the U.S. and a heavy diary of economic data which will throw more light on the inflation and interest rate outlook.

Wall Street got a boost from comments made by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday. Greenspan said he expected U.S. growth to decelerate later this year and the markets interpreted that to mean the Fed would not raise rates at the next FOMC meeting on May 20.
"The U.S. market clearly wants to go higher but will remain vulnerable to anything that suggests growth is strengthening," Jeffrey warned.
Back in the UK, major companies reporting next week include chemicals group BOC and food group Grand Metropolitan. Both are likely to show that the strong pound is hurting British exporters.
Elsewhere, results from BT, Cable & Wireless, Allied Domecq and supermarket group Safeway will provide a focus of interest.
